title: commodity brand positioning
primary_keyword: how to brand a commodity product
claim: Commodity products cannot win on product features, so positioning must create an operational risk for choosing anyone else.
hook: A commodity has no features to sell.

evidence.detail: Observed across multiple industrial supplier tenders where identical steel or chemical specifications force buyers to evaluate risk, logistics stability, and plant audit history rather than product performance.

slides.headline: A commodity has no features to sell.
When products are identical, marketing defaults to price.
slides.body: Lowering prices invites margin erosion and signals desperation to procurement committees.

slides.headline: Stop selling the steel. Start selling the certainty.
slides.body: Buyers do not risk their careers on the product. They risk their careers on whether the delivery arrives on Tuesday.

slides.headline: Positioning in industrial markets is risk transference.
slides.body: Your brand premium is insurance against plant downtime.

slides.headline: This requires abandoning half your product claims.
slides.body: Every page spent on technical specs is a page not spent on proving operational resilience.

items.label: Buyer Reality
items.detail: Wants proof of no line stoppages

slides.headline: Audit your collateral against one single question.
slides.body: Does this page prove our product is better, or does it prove our supply chain is unbreakable?

slides.headline: Commodity brands sell the sleep the buyer loses.
slides.body: Send this to whoever is tired of arguing about price in B2B procurement meetings.

caption:
A commodity has no features to sell.

Learning how to brand a commodity product starts with the buyer's delivery risk.

Most industrial marketers double down on technical datasheets. That fails because the procurement committee already has the ISO certificate on file.

They are not buying better steel. They are buying the elimination of plant downtime.

Positioning a commodity means making your competitors look like a logistical gamble.
